teaching.causalExplanation: Researching a skill starts with the question, and earlier you saw that the question decides everything after it. How do you get better at netball? That returns everything ever written, and answers nothing. How is shooting developed in netball? Better, but findings will clash, because they're about different learners. Here's a question you can research: how should practice be arranged to improve shooting under pressure, for teenage club netballers? It names the sport, the skill, the part of the skill, and who it's for. Pick a skill you can actually go and watch this week. Sources don't deserve equal weight, so rank them. At the top is a systematic review, which gathers every study on a question by a stated method. Next, a peer-reviewed study, checked by other researchers before it's published. Then textbooks and sporting bodies, accurate but often a few years behind. Then coaching magazines and journalism, written to be interesting, so the finding often sounds stronger than the study. And at the bottom, social media and coach opinion. Low doesn't mean worthless. A coach's opinion is weak evidence about what works, but strong evidence about what coaches do. Then ask four questions of any source. Who was studied? How many? Who paid for it? And is this the study, or someone's account of it? Now the four statements. Each one sits on real research, and three have been stretched. A: the real study found the best violinists had averaged about ten thousand hours of deliberate practice, effortful work on weaknesses with feedback, by about age twenty. An average became a requirement, and deliberate practice became just hours. C: elite athletes often did specialise early. But the ones who specialised and quit were never counted. That's a correlation, two things going together, read as a cause. Studies that follow everyone tend to favour trying several sports. D: visualising does help, alongside real practice, once you have a movement to rehearse. The qualifier got dropped. And the fourth stretch is a result from a narrow sample, say twelve elite adults, sold as true for everyone. B is the real finding. It's specific, it admits its own cost, and it's inconvenient: it tells coaches the better session looks worse. Convenient, round-numbered claims deserve the most suspicion. Even so, in real sport settings the effect is smaller than in the lab.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the four statements. Each one sits on real research, and three have been stretched. A: the real study found the best violinists had averaged about ten thousand hours of deliberate practice, effortful work on weaknesses with feedback, by about age twenty. An average became a requirement, and deliberate practice became just hours. C: elite athletes often did specialise early. But the ones who specialised and quit were never counted. That's a correlation, two things going together, read as a cause. Studies that follow everyone tend to favour trying several sports. D: visualising does help, alongside real practice, once you have a movement to rehearse. The qualifier got dropped. And the fourth stretch is a result from a narrow sample, say twelve elite adults, sold as true for everyone. B is the real finding. It's specific, it admits its own cost, and it's inconvenient: it tells coaches the better session looks worse. Convenient, round-numbered claims deserve the most suspicion. Even so, in real sport settings the effect is smaller than in the lab.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus asks how research is applied in practice. "Coaches should vary their practice" isn't an application. It's the finding with should added. An application is something you could photograph. Take the netball question. To acquire the shot, blocked practice while the pattern forms. To develop it, shuffle the three shooting drills by a called number instead of blocks of ten. To improve it, swap the cone for a live defender, so she has to choose between shooting and passing. Then add a limit. A session that looks worse can get dropped in a fortnight, and a finding from adult students might not hold for teenagers.

scenes.teachingReason: Then propose further research questions, which shows you actually read. Good questions come from four places.
